title.en: The Book Found Under a Shrine: The Discovery of the Per-t Em Hru
title.zh: 神龕下得書：《來日之書》之發現

region.en: The shrine of Hennu, Egypt (where the Book of the Dead was 'found' in the 1st Dynasty)
region.zh: 埃及赫努神龕（第一王朝時『發現』亡靈書處）

texts.period: Rubric of the Papyrus of Nu (BM 10477), tradition set in the 1st Dynasty (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. III)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. III, 'The Book Per-t em hru'

summary.en: The Book of the Dead's own discovery legend: a rubric states the text 'was discovered by a high official in the foundations of a shrine of the god Hennu during the reign of Semti, or Hesepti, a king of the 1st dynasty'; another says it was cut on the alabaster plinth of a statue of Mycerinus with letters inlaid in lapis lazuli, found by Prince Herutataf and exhibited to Khufu as 'a most wonderful thing' — a text that 'would make a man victorious upon earth and in the Other World... and would prevent him from dying the [second] death.'
summary.zh: 《亡靈書》自述之發現傳說：一條眉批云其書『乃一高官於第一王朝塞姆提王世，自赫努神龕之基下發得』；另一條則云其文『刻於門卡烏拉像之雪花石膏座上，字嵌青金石』，為胡夫王子赫魯塔塔夫所得，呈王以為『至奇之物』——其書『能使人在世與冥界皆得勝……並免遭第二次死亡』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient rubric tradition via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: One rubric in the Papyrus of Nu (Brit. Mus. No. 10477) states that the text of the work called 'PER-T EM HRU,' i.e., 'Coming Forth (or, into) the Day,' was discovered by a high official in the foundations of a shrine of the god Hennu during the reign of Semti, or Hesepti, a king of the 1st dynasty. Another rubric in the same papyrus says that the text was cut upon the alabaster plinth of a statue of Menkaura (Mycerinus), a king of the IVth dynasty, and that the letters were inlaid with lapis lazuli. The plinth was found by Prince Herutataf, a son of King Khufu (Cheops), who carried it off to his king and exhibited it as a 'most wonderful' thing.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. III.

passages.text: This composition was greatly reverenced, for it 'would make a man victorious upon earth and in the Other World; it would ensure him a safe and free passage through the Tuat (Under World); it would allow him to go in and to go out, and to take at any time any form he pleased; it would make his soul to flourish, and would prevent him from dying the [second] death.' For the deceased to receive the full benefit of this text it had to be recited by a man 'who was ceremonially pure, and who had not eaten fish or meat, and had not consorted with women.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. III.

title.en: A Seat in the Boat of Millions of Years

region.en: The sky-river of Ra, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界拉之天河水道

texts.period: Book of the Dead chs. 101-102, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the chapters of the Boat of Ra

summary.en: The great ambition of the blessed dead: chapters 101 and 102 of the Book of the Dead 'provided access for him to the Boat of Ra' — the Boat of Millions of Years in which the sun crosses the sky-river daily — the same boat that stopped its course when Horus lay dead (cut in the Horus record) and that the scribe Ani begged: 'Let there be prepared for me a seat in the Boat of Ra on the day when the god goeth forth.'
summary.zh: 蒙福亡者之大志：亡靈書第一〇一至一〇二章『使其得登拉之舟』——即日日渡天河之『百萬年之舟』——即荷魯斯死時為之停駛之舟（見荷魯斯之死條），亦書吏阿尼所求：『當神出行之日，願為我備拉舟中之一席。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 101 and 102 provided access for him to the Boat of Ra. Chaps. 108, 109, 112, and 116 enabled him to know the Souls (i.e. gods) of the East and West, and of the towns of Pe, Nekhen, Khemenu, and Anu.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary.

passages.text: Let there be prepared for me a seat in the Boat of Ra on the day when the god goeth forth. Let me be received into the presence of Osiris, in the Land where Truth is spoken.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IV, the prayer of Ani (Book of the Dead ch. 15).

title.en: Nephthys the Barren Shore: Anubis Born of the Overflow
title.zh: 荒岸奈芙蒂斯：因氾濫而生之安努畢斯

region.en: The sea-shore and desert edges of Egypt (the land Nephthys represents)
region.zh: 埃及海岸與大漠之緣（奈芙蒂斯所象之地）

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXXVIII

summary.en: The allegory of the fourth sister: 'Horus, the offspring of Osiris, the Nile, and Isis, the Earth, was born in the marshes of Buto, because the vapour of damp land destroys drought. Nephthys, or Teleute, represents the extreme limits of the country and the sea-shore, that is, barren land. Osiris (i.e., the Nile) overflowed this barren land, and Anubis was the result.'
summary.zh: 四姊妹之寓言：『荷魯斯——尼羅（奧西里斯）與土（伊西斯）之子——生於布托之沼，蓋濕地之氣克旱。奈芙蒂斯（或名特琉忒）則象國之極限與海岸，即不毛之地。尼羅（奧西里斯）氾濫於此荒岸，遂生安努畢斯。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient allegoresis via Plutarch (Budge's summary of sec. XXXVIII); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Horus, the offspring of Osiris, the Nile, and Isis, the Earth, was born in the marshes of Buto, because the vapour of damp land destroys drought. Nephthys, or Teleute, represents the extreme limits of the country and the sea-shore, that is, barren land. Osiris (i.e., the Nile) overflowed this barren land, and Anubis was the result.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXXVIII (Budge's summary).

title.en: Seventeen Thousand Years of Heracles: The Seniority of the Egyptian Gods
title.zh: 一萬七千年之海拉克勒斯：埃及諸神之年資

region.en: Egypt and Tyre (Herodotus' inquiry into the age of the gods)
region.zh: 埃及與推羅（希羅多德究神祇之年壽）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.43-44 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 43-44

summary.en: Herodotus' pilgrimage of antiquity: in Egypt Heracles is one of the twelve gods, seventeen thousand years old by the priests' reckoning; sailing to Tyre he found the temple of Heracles 'set up at the same time when Tyre was founded... a period of two thousand three hundred years', and at Thasos a Heracles-temple five generations before the son of Amphitryon was born — 'So then my inquiries show clearly that Heracles is an ancient god.'
summary.zh: 希羅多德考神祇年壽之旅：於埃及，海拉克勒斯列十二神之數，祭司推算距今一萬七千年；至推羅，見其廟『與推羅建城同時……二千三百年』；於塔索斯，其廟早於安菲特里翁之子誕生五代——『我之查究明證：海拉克勒斯乃古之神也。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient comparative inquiry via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: About Heracles I heard the account given that he was of the number of the twelve gods; but of the other Heracles whom the Hellenes know I was not able to hear in any part of Egypt... In fact however Heracles is a very ancient Egyptian god; and (as they say themselves) it is seventeen thousand years to the beginning of the reign of Amasis from the time when the twelve gods, of whom they count that Heracles is one, were begotten of the eight gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.43.

passages.text: I made a voyage also to Tyre of Phenicia, hearing that in that place there was a holy temple of Heracles; and I saw that it was richly furnished with many votive offerings besides, and especially there were in it two pillars, the one of pure gold and the other of an emerald stone of such size as to shine by night: and having come to speech with the priests of the god, I asked them how long time it was since their temple had been set up: and these also I found to be at variance with the Hellenes, for they said that at the same time when Tyre was founded, the temple of the god also had been set up, and that it was a period of two thousand three hundred years since their people began to dwell at Tyre.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.44.

passages.text: So then my inquiries show clearly that Heracles is an ancient god, and those of the Hellenes seem to me to act most rightly who have two temples of Heracles set up, and who sacrifice to the one as an immortal god and with the title Olympian, and make offerings of the dead to the other as a hero.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.44.

title.en: The Colchians of Sesostris: Circumcision, Linen, and Kinship Across the Sea
title.zh: 塞索斯特里斯之科爾基斯人：割禮、亞麻與跨海血緣

region.en: Colchis at the river Phasis, at the far end of Sesostris' march
region.zh: 法西斯河畔科爾基斯（塞索斯特里斯遠征之極處）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.104-105 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 104-105

summary.en: Herodotus' proof that an Egyptian army once reached the Black Sea: the Colchians 'are evidently Egyptian', dark-skinned and curly-haired — 'but also still more because the Colchians, Egyptians, and Ethiopians alone of all the races of men have practised circumcision from the first' — and 'they alone work flax in the same fashion as the Egyptians', weaving the linen called Sardonic in Hellas and Egyptian in Egypt.
summary.zh: 希羅多德證埃及大軍曾達黑海：科爾基斯人『顯為埃及人』——膚黑髮卷，『尤以科爾基斯、埃及與埃塞俄比亞三者為世上最初行割禮之族』——且『彼等織亞麻之法，與埃及人全同』，所織者在希臘稱薩爾多尼克、在埃及稱埃及麻布。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic argument via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The Colchian claim became a set-piece of the Sesostris legend.

passages.text: For the people of Colchis are evidently Egyptian, and this I perceived for myself before I heard it from others. So when I had come to consider the matter I asked them both; and the Colchians had remembrance of the Egyptians more than the Egyptians of the Colchians; but the Egyptians said they believed that the Colchians were a portion of the army of Sesostris. That this was so I conjectured myself not only because they are dark-skinned and have curly hair (this of itself amounts to nothing, for there are other races which are so), but also still more because the Colchians, Egyptians, and Ethiopians alone of all the races of men have practised circumcision from the first.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.104.

passages.text: Now let me tell another thing about the Colchians to show how they resemble the Egyptians: — they alone work flax in the same fashion as the Egyptians, and the two nations are like one another in their whole manner of living and also in their language: now the linen of Colchis is called by the Hellenes Sardonic, whereas that from Egypt is called Egyptian.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.105.

title.en: No Text Has His History: Osiris Usurps the Powers of All Other Gods
title.zh: 無一書載其史：奧西里斯兼眾神之權

region.en: Egypt, all periods (the rise of the Osiris cult)
region.zh: 埃及歷代（奧西里斯祭之興）

texts.period: Synthesis from texts of every period (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. I)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, 'The History of Osiris as told by Classical Writers' (preface)

summary.en: The missing biography of Egypt's greatest god: 'In no text do we find any connected history of the god, and nowhere are stated in detail the reasons why he assumed his exalted position as the judge of souls... No funerary inscription exists, however early, in which evidence cannot be found proving that the deceased had set his hope of immortality in Osiris' — and 'it is Osiris who is made to usurp the attributes and powers of other gods', his cult growing 'in proportion to the growth of the power and wealth' of Egypt itself.
summary.zh: 埃及至大神之『失傳列傳』：『無一文本載其連貫之史，亦無一處詳述其何以居亡魂判官之尊位……無論何古之葬銘，皆可證亡者以不朽之望寄於奧西里斯』——且『乃奧西里斯兼他神之性與權』，其祭之盛『與埃及國勢財力之盛並進』。

sensitivity.note: Egyptological synthesis via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The religious literature of all the great periods of Egyptian history is filled with allusions to incidents connected with the life, death, and resurrection of Osiris, the god and judge of the Egyptian dead; and from first to last the authors of religious texts took it for granted that their readers were well acquainted with such incidents in all their details. In no text do we find any connected history of the god, and nowhere are stated in detail the reasons why he assumed his exalted position as the judge of souls, or why, for about four thousand years, he remained the great type and symbol of the Resurrection.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.

passages.text: No funerary inscription exists, however early, in which evidence cannot be found proving that the deceased had set his hope of immortality in Osiris, and at no time in Egypt's long history do we find that the position of Osiris was usurped by any other god. On the contrary, it is Osiris who is made to usurp the attributes and powers of other gods, and in tracing his history in the following pages we shall find that the importance of the cult of this god grew in proportion to the growth of the power and wealth of the country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.
